title: Habeas corpus during the Emergency
body: During the Emergency the government made extensive use of preventive detention laws, and thousands of political workers were arrested. Many petitions were filed in the High Courts by and on behalf of the detained persons. The government argued that during the Emergency it was not even necessary to tell an arrested person the reasons and grounds of the arrest, and that such persons could not approach the courts. Several High Courts disagreed and held that even after the declaration of Emergency a court could hear a writ of habeas corpus filed by a person challenging his or her detention. In April 1976 the constitution bench of the Supreme Court over-ruled the High Courts and accepted the government's plea. After the Emergency, the courts took a far more active role in protecting the civil liberties of individuals, and many civil liberties organisations came up.

title: The verdict of 1977
body: In January 1977, after eighteen months of Emergency, the government announced Lok Sabha elections, which were held in March. The major opposition parties came together to form the Janata Party and turned the campaign into a referendum on the Emergency. For the first time since Independence the Congress was defeated in Lok Sabha elections. It won only 154 seats, and its share of votes fell to less than 35 per cent. The Janata Party and its allies won 330 of the 542 seats, of which the Janata Party itself won 295. In north India the Congress lost every constituency in Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, Delhi, Haryana and Punjab, while it virtually swept the southern States.
